newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Welding believed to have caused HK inferno.
newsitem.headline: Welding believed to have caused HK inferno.

text.p: Welding in lift shafts was the possible cause of Hong Kong's worst-ever building blaze, which killed at least 39 people, a senior fire official said on Thursday.

"An eye witness claimed that welding work was in progress in one of the lift shafts...and that a spark from the welding ignited combustibles at the bottom of the shafts," fire chief Peter Cheung told a news conference.
That might have started the fire which spread quickly from the ground right up to the top floors, he added.
But investigations were continuing into the cause, he stressed.
The fire brigade had set up two special teams to look into the fire's cause and the reasons for its fast spread and the great number of casualities.
"...it may well be the case that we will feel and the community will feel that there should be a full commision of inquiry under a judge," Governor Chris Patten told legislators.
But whether that happens would depend on the outcome of the fire services' review, he added.
The fire engulfed a 16-floor shop and office block in a bustling Hong Kong tourist district, killing at least 39 people and injuring 81 others, of whom 46 were still in hospital.
It broke out late on Wednesday afternoon and rapidly gutted the first four storeys before racing up the lift shaft to the top three floors.
It was extinguished early Thursday afternoon after raging for more than 21 hours.
The closed design of the department store at the bottom of the building on Nathan Road, Kowloon, was believed to be a big factor in the fast spread of the fire, Cheung said.
With all the store's windows sealed, the heat and smoke could only billow up the building's two staircases, quickly taking the blaze to the top floors, he said.
The situation was worsened by the lack of an up-to-date fire protection system in the building, Cheung added. Many older buildings in Hong Kong have few, if any, anti-fire devices.
Patten pressed for the speedy passage of legislation to tighten fire regulations.
Hong Kong's worst fire on record was in 1918 when 600 people were killed and 400 injured in a blaze at the Happy Valley Race course on Hong Kong Island.
